locations.name: Osaka
locations.blurb: Japan's kitchen and its loudest city — a merchant town rather than an imperial one, flat, neon-lit and much less formal than Kyoto an hour away. Everything here points at food and at the canal-side signs above Dotonbori.
locations.fun_fact: Osaka's motto is *kuidaore* — roughly 'eat yourself bankrupt' — and the city takes it seriously enough that the Glico running man sign over the Ebisu bridge has been relit six times since 1935.

locations.name: Mount Fuji
locations.blurb: A near-perfect volcanic cone of 3,776 m, visible from Tokyo on a clear winter morning and hidden behind cloud for much of the summer. It has been climbed as a pilgrimage for over a thousand years and painted more often than any other mountain on Earth.
locations.fun_fact: Fuji is still an active volcano; its last eruption, in 1707, dropped ash on Edo 100 km away for two weeks and left the Hōei crater on the southeastern flank that you can see from the Tokaido line.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The official climbing season is only July to early September. Outside it the huts are shut and the mountain is a serious winter ascent — but the Chureito Pagoda view is best in the cold months anyway.

locations.name: Beijing
locations.blurb: The capital, and the one Chinese city built to be looked at from above: a grid of concentric ring roads laid around the Forbidden City on a north–south axis a Ming emperor set. Twenty-two million people, six hundred years of imperial architecture, and the best subway in the country underneath it.
locations.fun_fact: The Forbidden City has 980 surviving buildings and was the seat of 24 emperors across the Ming and Qing dynasties. It was closed to ordinary Chinese people for nearly five centuries.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Skip Wangfujing and walk the hutongs between Nanluoguxiang and the Drum Tower at seven in the morning, when the lanes belong to people buying breakfast rather than to tour groups.

locations.name: Shanghai
locations.blurb: China's largest city and its money: colonial stone along the Bund on one bank, the Pudong skyline answering it across the Huangpu on the other. Between them sits the densest concentration of twentieth-century Chinese history anywhere, most of it still standing and lived in.
locations.fun_fact: Pudong was farmland and warehouses until 1990. Everything in that skyline — Jin Mao, the World Financial Center, the 632-metre Shanghai Tower — went up inside one working lifetime.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The former French Concession is the part people miss. Walk Wukang Road and Anfu Road under the plane trees; the lane-house neighbourhoods behind them are the real city.

locations.name: Great Wall at Badaling
locations.blurb: The restored section of the Great Wall closest to Beijing, about 70 km northwest of the city, and the one nearly every first-time visitor sees. Steep, cable-car served, comprehensively rebuilt, and on a good day extremely crowded — which is itself part of what makes it worth seeing.
locations.fun_fact: Badaling opened to visitors in 1958 and has since received hundreds of heads of state. Richard Nixon walked it in 1972, on the trip that reopened relations between China and the United States.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Turn left at the top of the stairs, not right. The north side is the famous photograph; the south side is steeper, quieter, and has the better view back down the valley.

locations.name: Xi'an
locations.blurb: The eastern end of the Silk Road and capital of thirteen Chinese dynasties, including the Tang. It still has its full Ming city wall — fourteen kilometres of it, wide enough to cycle — and a Muslim Quarter that has been feeding travellers for well over a thousand years.
locations.fun_fact: The Terracotta Army was found in 1974 by farmers digging a well. There are more than 8,000 figures, and every face is different.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Rent a bike on top of the city wall at dusk and ride the full circuit. It takes under two hours and it is the only way to understand how the grid below you was laid out.

locations.name: Guilin
locations.blurb: The city at the head of the karst country: limestone towers standing straight up out of flat ground and out of the Li River itself, in the landscape Chinese ink painters have been drawing for a thousand years. Most people use it as the gateway and go downstream.
locations.fun_fact: The back of the ¥20 note is a view of the Li River karst at Xingping, an hour downstream. People hold the banknote up to line it against the actual hills.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Guilin itself is a working provincial city. Sleep in Yangshuo or Xingping instead and wake up inside the scenery rather than an hour's bus ride from it.

locations.name: Hong Kong
locations.blurb: Seven and a half million people on 1,100 square kilometres of which three quarters is undeveloped: mountain, country park and outlying island. A British colony until 1997 and now a Special Administrative Region, it runs its own currency, its own law and the world's busiest cross-harbour ferry.
locations.fun_fact: Hong Kong has more skyscrapers than any other city on earth — well over 500 buildings above 150 metres, roughly double New York's count.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Star Ferry across Victoria Harbour still costs a few Hong Kong dollars and is the best view in the city. Sit on the lower deck, and go at dusk.

locations.name: Guangzhou
locations.blurb: Canton: the third of China's four Tier 1 cities, the oldest continuously open port in the country, and the capital of Cantonese food. Eighteen million people on the Pearl River, at the head of a delta that manufactures a large share of everything you own.
locations.fun_fact: The Canton Fair has been held here since 1957 and is the largest trade fair in China — for decades it was effectively the only door between Chinese factories and foreign buyers.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Have breakfast dim sum somewhere old on Enning Road, then walk the arcaded qilou shophouse streets around it. This is where Cantonese cooking is from, and locals eat at 8 a.m., not at noon.

locations.name: Shenzhen
locations.blurb: The fastest-built big city in human history. In 1980 this was a county of fishing and farming villages next to the Hong Kong border; it was made China's first Special Economic Zone and is now a Tier 1 city of more than seventeen million with the country's densest concentration of hardware engineering.
locations.fun_fact: Huaqiangbei is a district of multi-storey electronics markets where you can buy any component of a phone individually — and, famously, have a prototype built from them in an afternoon.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Shenzhen has almost no old town, so go up instead: the free observation floor politics change, but Lianhuashan Park's hill gives you the whole Futian skyline for nothing, and it is where the city goes at dusk.

locations.name: Chengdu
locations.blurb: The capital of Sichuan and the city everyone names first among the 'new first-tier' — twenty-one million people, a teahouse culture that refuses to hurry, and the hottest food in China. It has been continuously inhabited on the same site for more than two thousand years.
locations.fun_fact: Chengdu sits in a basin so persistently overcast that clear views of the 7,500-metre peaks 100 km west are rare enough that people post photographs when the mountains appear.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Go to People's Park in the morning and pay for a bamboo chair, a glass of jasmine tea and a man with tweezers to clean your ears. It is not a tourist show; it is what Chengdu does with a free morning.

locations.name: Chongqing
locations.blurb: A city built on cliffs where the Jialing meets the Yangtze, stacked so steeply that a road can be the roof of the building below it and a monorail runs through an apartment block. Administratively it is a municipality the size of Austria; the actual city holds about nine million.
locations.fun_fact: Chongqing was China's wartime capital from 1938 to 1946, and the tunnels dug into its cliffs as bomb shelters are now used as restaurants, bars and hotpot halls.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Ride the Yangtze River Cableway across the water at night, then find the Liziba station where the light rail goes straight through the sixth to eighth floors of a residential tower.

locations.name: Hangzhou
locations.blurb: The city Marco Polo called the finest in the world, wrapped around the willows and causeways of West Lake. Southern Song capital, home of Longjing green tea, and now the head office of China's largest e-commerce company — a 'new first-tier' city that still looks like a painting.
locations.fun_fact: West Lake has been deliberately landscaped for over a thousand years. Su Causeway is named for the poet-governor Su Shi, who had it built out of mud dredged from the lake in 1090.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk up into the tea terraces at Longjing village behind the lake. The hills are working farms, the villages sell their own leaf, and almost nobody on the lakeshore bothers to climb.

locations.name: Suzhou
locations.blurb: Canals, walled gardens and silk, half an hour from Shanghai by train. Founded in 514 BC on the Grand Canal, Suzhou spent centuries as the wealthiest city in China and put the money into scholar-gardens; nine of them are now a single World Heritage listing.
locations.fun_fact: The Humble Administrator's Garden is neither humble nor small — about five hectares, roughly a fifth of it water — and it has been rebuilt repeatedly since 1509.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The gardens are ticketed and busy; the canal lanes are free and are not. Walk Pingjiang Road early, then cut into the residential alleys west of it where the bridges still have laundry over them.

locations.name: Nanjing
locations.blurb: The southern capital: seat of six dynasties, the Ming founder's tomb, and the Republic of China's capital before 1949. It still has the longest surviving city wall in the world and a boulevard of plane trees planted to shade it.
locations.fun_fact: The Ming city wall was over 35 km long and much of it stands; the bricks are stamped with the names of the kilns and workmen who made them, so responsibility for a bad brick could be traced.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Climb onto the wall at Zhonghua Gate and look at the gate's structure itself — four successive archways with chambers between them, built to trap an attacking force inside.

locations.name: Wuhan
locations.blurb: Three cities in one — Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang — sitting where the Han River joins the Yangtze, which makes it the transport hinge of central China. Eleven million people, dozens of universities, and the first bridge ever thrown across the lower Yangtze.
locations.fun_fact: The 1911 uprising that ended two thousand years of dynastic rule started in Wuchang, on this side of the river.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Wuhan's breakfast is the point: find a stall doing reganmian, the dry sesame noodles the city eats standing up, and go before nine.

locations.blurb: Beijing's port, thirty minutes away by high-speed rail, and the strangest architectural collection in China: nine foreign concessions carved out between 1860 and 1902 each built in its own national style, so a Italianate street runs into a German one.
locations.fun_fact: Tianjin's Five Great Avenues district holds more than two thousand surviving Western-style villas from the concession era.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Cross the Hai River at night for the Tianjin Eye — a Ferris wheel built into a road bridge, which is not a thing that exists anywhere else.

locations.name: Qingdao
locations.blurb: A German colony from 1898 to 1914, which is why a Chinese port city on the Yellow Sea has red-tiled roofs, a Lutheran church, cobbled hill streets and the country's most famous brewery. Beaches, headlands and the best seafood on the northern coast.
locations.fun_fact: Tsingtao beer has been brewed here since 1903 to the German original, and locals buy it by the litre in plastic bags from corner shops with a tap.

locations.name: Changsha
locations.blurb: The capital of Hunan, and the city that currently sets China's consumer trends — the milk-tea chains, the variety television, the night markets that stay open until four. Also the hottest-eating province in the country, which is saying something in China.
locations.fun_fact: The 2,200-year-old Mawangdui tombs were excavated here and produced the best-preserved ancient human body ever found, along with silk documents that rewrote parts of early Chinese history.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Cross to Orange Isle in the middle of the Xiang River at night, then eat stinky tofu and crayfish on Pozi Street until you lose track of the hour. The city genuinely does not sleep.

locations.blurb: The rail junction of China — where the country's main north–south and east–west lines cross — and the capital of Henan, the province with the deepest layer of early Chinese history under it. Ten million people, and almost no one visits on purpose.
locations.fun_fact: Foxconn's Zhengzhou plant has assembled a large share of the world's iPhones, at times employing well over 200,000 people on one site.

locations.blurb: The old Manchu capital and the capital of the northeast rust belt: the Qing dynasty started here, before it took Beijing, and its palace is still standing. Heavy industry, brutal winters, and the warmest street food culture in China.
locations.fun_fact: The Mukden Palace is the only surviving imperial palace complex in China outside Beijing — the Qing built it before they had the Forbidden City.

locations.blurb: One of the busiest ports on earth by tonnage, and an old one — Ningbo was trading with Japan and Korea a thousand years ago. Behind the container terminals sits the oldest surviving private library in Asia and a quiet, prosperous merchant city.
locations.fun_fact: The Tianyi Pavilion library was built in 1561 and still holds its collection. Its water pool was designed as fire protection for the books.

locations.blurb: The factory floor of the Pearl River Delta: ten million people, most of them migrants, in a city with no real centre — a continuous sprawl of industrial towns each specialising in one product. If you own something mass-produced, some of it plausibly passed through here.
locations.fun_fact: Dongguan is administered as a prefecture-level city with no districts or counties beneath it, so its towns report straight to the city — a structure built for factories rather than for citizens.

locations.name: Foshan
locations.blurb: Guangzhou's neighbour, effectively fused to it, and the home town of southern Chinese martial arts — Wong Fei-hung and Ip Man both came from here, which is why half the kung fu films ever made are set in it. Also China's ceramics capital for the last five centuries.
locations.fun_fact: Ip Man, who taught Bruce Lee, was born in Foshan. The city has a museum to him next to the ancestral temple.

locations.fun_fact: Hefei hosts the Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak, a fusion reactor that has held plasma above 100 million degrees for minutes at a time.

locations.fun_fact: During the Second World War Kunming was the eastern terminus of the Burma Road and of 'the Hump' airlift over the Himalaya, and the base for the Flying Tigers.

locations.fun_fact: The Harbin Ice and Snow Festival builds a temporary city of full-size illuminated buildings out of blocks cut from the Songhua River, and it is one of the largest ice festivals in the world.

locations.name: Dalian
locations.blurb: A port on the tip of the Liaodong peninsula that Russia built, Japan took, and both left their street plans in — European roundabouts and squares, unusual in a Chinese city. Cool summers, a rocky coast road, and the best shellfish in the northeast.
locations.fun_fact: Zhongshan Square is a ten-street radial roundabout laid out under Russian and then Japanese administration, ringed by banks and hotels from that period.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Ride the surviving 1909 tram line across town, then take the coastal road southeast to Fujiazhuang for the swimming — it is a pebble cove rather than a resort beach.

locations.name: Xiamen
locations.blurb: An island city facing Taiwan across the strait, and one of the most liveable places in China: sea on every side, no heavy industry in the centre, and a ring road you can cycle. It was a treaty port, so the architecture is half-colonial and unusually pretty.
locations.fun_fact: Gulangyu, the small island offshore, has no cars at all and about a thousand surviving colonial-era villas. It is a World Heritage Site.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Everyone ferries to Gulangyu. Fewer people walk the Shapowei fishing harbour and the old campus of Xiamen University next to it, which is arguably the handsomest university in the country.

locations.name: Fuzhou
locations.blurb: Fujian's capital, an old port up the Min River, and the ancestral home of a very large share of the Chinese diaspora in North America and Southeast Asia. Banyan trees everywhere — the city's nickname is 'Banyan City' — and a restored quarter of Ming and Qing lanes in the middle.
locations.fun_fact: Sanfang Qixiang, the 'three lanes and seven alleys', preserves a district of lane houses where an extraordinary number of late-Qing reformers, admirals and scholars were born.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The hot springs are municipal and cheap — Fuzhou is built over them, and the public bathhouses in the old town have been running for generations.

locations.name: Jinan
locations.blurb: The 'City of Springs': more than a hundred artesian springs rise inside Jinan, and the old town is built around the pools they fill. Shandong's capital, an hour and a half from Beijing by fast train, and the gateway to Mount Tai and Qufu.
locations.fun_fact: Baotu Spring has been ranked the finest of the springs since imperial times, and locals still queue at public taps around the old town to fill bottles with spring water for tea.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Follow the moat walk around Daming Lake at six in the morning. The springs feed it, the water is clear, and the whole old city is out doing tai chi beside it.

locations.name: Wuxi
locations.blurb: On the northern shore of Lake Tai between Suzhou and Nanjing — a wealthy manufacturing city that most travellers pass through at 300 km/h without stopping. Its name means 'without tin', after the mines that ran out two thousand years ago.
locations.fun_fact: The purple-clay teapots that serious Chinese tea drinkers use come from Yixing, in Wuxi's territory, where they have been made since the Song dynasty.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take the causeway out into Lake Tai at Yuantouzhu when the cherry blossom is out; then go to Yixing and watch a potter throw a zisha pot by hand.

locations.name: Wenzhou
locations.blurb: A coastal city hemmed in by mountains, historically cut off from the rest of China by land, which turned it into the most entrepreneurial place in the country — the 'Wenzhou model' of private family firms and informal lending is a chapter in every Chinese economics textbook.
locations.fun_fact: The Wenzhou dialect is so far from Mandarin, and from its own neighbours, that it is frequently described as the hardest Chinese variety for other Chinese speakers to understand.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Go up the Nanxi River valley an hour north for the ancient villages and covered bridges of Yongjia — timber-frame lanes and swimming holes that see almost no foreign visitors at all.

locations.blurb: China's Detroit — the First Automobile Works has been building cars here since 1953 — and before that the capital of Japanese-occupied Manchukuo, whose puppet emperor's palace is still standing on the edge of the centre.
locations.fun_fact: Puyi, the last Qing emperor, spent 1934–45 in Changchun as the nominal ruler of Manchukuo. His palace is now a museum about exactly how little power he had.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Japanese-built government quarter along Xinmin Street is an intact 1930s planned district that almost nobody walks — heavy stone ministries, now hospitals and university buildings.

locations.blurb: A village of a few hundred households in 1900 that became a railway junction and is now a provincial capital of eleven million — the clearest example in China of a city that exists because two lines crossed. Pharmaceuticals, textiles, and no old town whatsoever.
locations.fun_fact: Shijiazhuang's growth is so recent that its name still means what it meant when it was a hamlet: 'Shi family village'.

locations.name: Taiyuan
locations.blurb: The capital of Shanxi, which sits on China's biggest coal reserves and has paid for it in air. It is also the gateway to the densest collection of surviving ancient buildings in the country — Shanxi holds the majority of China's pre-1300 timber architecture.
locations.fun_fact: Shanxi has roughly three quarters of all surviving Chinese wooden buildings older than the Ming dynasty, because the dry climate and the province's poverty left them alone.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Jinci Temple on the southwestern edge of the city has Song-dynasty halls and painted figures from 1087 still in place. Then eat the noodles — Shanxi makes more shapes of them than anywhere else.

locations.name: Nanchang
locations.blurb: Jiangxi's capital on the Gan River, just south of Poyang Lake — the largest freshwater lake in China and a wintering ground for most of the world's Siberian cranes. In Chinese political history it is where the People's Liberation Army dates its founding.
locations.fun_fact: The Tengwang Pavilion has been destroyed and rebuilt 29 times since AD 653; the current version is from 1989, and is famous mostly because of a 7th-century poem written about the previous one.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Go out to Poyang Lake in December or January. Almost the entire world population of Siberian cranes winters there, and hardly anyone is watching them.

locations.name: Guiyang
locations.blurb: The capital of Guizhou, a poor mountain province that has become the site of China's data centres — cool, stable, seismically quiet and full of cheap hydropower. Overcast most of the year, ringed by karst, and the best base for the Miao and Dong country to the east.
locations.fun_fact: The 500-metre FAST radio telescope, the largest single-dish radio telescope in the world, was built in a natural karst sinkhole about 170 km from Guiyang.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Qingyan, a walled Ming garrison town, is 30 km south and gets a fraction of the visitors that a comparable place in Jiangsu would. Eat the sour fish soup.

locations.name: Nanning
locations.blurb: Guangxi's capital, 160 km from Vietnam, subtropical and green enough to be called the Green City. It is the permanent host of the China–ASEAN Expo, which makes it the country's front door to Southeast Asia by land.
locations.fun_fact: Guangxi is an autonomous region of the Zhuang, who at roughly eighteen million people are the largest ethnic minority in China.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take the train southwest to the Detian waterfall on the Vietnamese border, where the falls are split between two countries and you can raft to the line in the middle.

locations.name: Lanzhou
locations.blurb: A city squeezed into a narrow valley where the Yellow River cuts through the loess — long, thin, and the first Chinese city the river passes through. Historically the crossing point for everything going west along the Silk Road, and the noodle capital of the country.
locations.fun_fact: Lanzhou beef noodles are eaten for breakfast and are so standardised that a customer orders by noodle width, from thread-thin to belt-flat.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk down to the Yellow River waterfront for the 1909 Zhongshan Bridge and the sheepskin rafts — inflated hides lashed to a frame, still used to ferry people across.

locations.name: Ürümqi
locations.blurb: The capital of Xinjiang and, by most measures, the city furthest from any ocean on earth. It is where Han China meets Central Asia: Uyghur, Kazakh, Hui and Han in one city, on the north side of the Tianshan range.
locations.fun_fact: Ürümqi is about 2,500 km from the nearest coastline, which makes it the most landlocked major city in the world.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Xinjiang officially runs on Beijing time, two hours ahead of the sun here, so much of the city keeps an unofficial local clock. Expect dinner at ten and daylight at eleven in summer.

locations.name: Xining
locations.blurb: Qinghai's capital at 2,300 metres, on the edge of the Tibetan plateau — the last low-altitude city on the railway to Lhasa, and the sensible place to acclimatise. Han, Hui and Tibetan in roughly equal measure, with the mosque and the monastery a short bus ride apart.
locations.fun_fact: Kumbum Monastery, 25 km outside the city, is one of the six great Gelug monasteries and stands on the birthplace of Tsongkhapa, the school's founder.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Spend two nights here before going higher, and use one of them on the night market — Qinghai's lamb, yoghurt and hand-pulled noodles are the reason people in Xining are cheerful about the altitude.

locations.name: Hohhot
locations.blurb: The capital of Inner Mongolia, whose Mongolian name means 'blue city'. Tibetan-Buddhist temples from the Ming, a Qing-era Muslim quarter, China's dairy industry headquarters, and grassland starting about an hour north of the ring road.
locations.fun_fact: Inner Mongolia produces a large share of China's milk — both Yili and Mengniu, the country's two dairy giants, are headquartered in Hohhot.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Go to the Xilamuren or Gegentala grassland on a weekday rather than a weekend, and stay overnight in a ger. The day-trip version is a performance; the night is not.

locations.name: Quanzhou
locations.blurb: Marco Polo's Zayton, and in the Song and Yuan dynasties one of the greatest ports in the world — the Chinese end of the maritime Silk Road. It kept the religious archaeology to prove it: mosques, Hindu carvings, Nestorian and Manichaean remains, all in one Fujianese city.
locations.fun_fact: The Qingjing Mosque was founded in 1009 and is the oldest surviving mosque in China; Quanzhou also holds the world's only known surviving Manichaean temple still in use.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Quanzhou became a World Heritage Site in 2021 and is still not on most itineraries. Walk Xijie at night for the puppet theatres and the oyster-shell walls of Xunpu village on the coast.

locations.name: Pingyao
locations.blurb: A complete walled Ming and Qing county town, six kilometres of fortification with the streets inside intact — the best-preserved traditional city in China, largely because Shanxi was too poor to modernise it. In the 19th century it was the country's banking centre.
locations.fun_fact: Rishengchang, on the main street, was China's first draft bank, founded here around 1823. For a while Pingyao handled a large share of the empire's remittances.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Stay inside the walls in a courtyard inn and walk the ramparts at dawn. By ten the day-trippers arrive from Taiyuan; before that the town is just people opening shops.

locations.blurb: A coal city on the edge of Inner Mongolia that happens to sit beside two of the greatest things in Chinese art: the Yungang Grottoes and, an hour south, the Hanging Monastery pinned to a cliff. Its old town wall has been controversially and comprehensively rebuilt.
locations.fun_fact: Datong was the capital of the Northern Wei in the 5th century, which is why the Buddhist carving here predates almost everything comparable further south.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Hanging Temple at Hengshan is held to the rock face by wooden beams driven into the cliff and has stood for about 1,500 years. Go early; the walkways only take a few people at a time.

locations.name: Luoyang
locations.blurb: Capital of thirteen dynasties and for long stretches the largest city in the world, on the Luo River in the Yellow River heartland. What survives above ground is mostly Buddhist: the Longmen Grottoes downstream and the first Buddhist temple built in China.
locations.fun_fact: White Horse Temple, founded in AD 68, is traditionally held to be the first Buddhist temple in China — Buddhism entered the country through this city.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Come in mid-April for the peony festival. Luoyang has grown peonies since the Tang dynasty and the whole city turns out for it, which almost no foreign itinerary accounts for.

locations.name: Dunhuang
locations.blurb: An oasis town at the western end of the Hexi Corridor where the Silk Road split to go round the Taklamakan. Sand dunes come right up to the edge of town, there is a spring-fed crescent lake among them, and the Mogao Caves are 25 km southeast.
locations.fun_fact: The Library Cave at Mogao, sealed around the 11th century and opened in 1900, held some 50,000 manuscripts — including the world's earliest dated printed book, from AD 868.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Climb Mingsha Shan for sunset, then come back into town for the night market — Dunhuang eats donkey-meat noodles, and the market runs late because the afternoon is too hot to be outside.

locations.name: Jiayuguan
locations.blurb: The western end of the Ming Great Wall: a fortress in the narrowest part of the Hexi Corridor, with desert on one side and the snow of the Qilian range on the other. For centuries this gate was the edge of China, and exile beyond it was a sentence.
locations.fun_fact: The Overhanging Great Wall northwest of the fort climbs a bare ridge at a brutal angle — the wall here is rammed earth, not brick, because there was nothing else to build with.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Drive south to the Qilian foothills and the July First Glacier road. The contrast — fort, gravel desert, then 4,000-metre ice — is the whole point of the place.

locations.fun_fact: The clay Sleeping Buddha in Dafo Temple is about 35 metres long and dates from 1098. It is still in its original hall.

locations.name: Kashgar
locations.blurb: The westernmost city in China, closer to Kabul than to Beijing, where the northern and southern Silk Road routes around the Taklamakan met again. A Uyghur city of mud-brick lanes, the largest mosque in the country, and roads over the Pamirs to Pakistan and Kyrgyzstan.
locations.fun_fact: Kashgar has been a trading city for more than two thousand years. Its Sunday livestock market is still a working market where people come in from the countryside to buy sheep, not to be photographed.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Karakoram Highway south towards Tashkurgan and the Khunjerab Pass is one of the great drives on earth — Karakul lake sits at 3,600 metres under two 7,500-metre peaks about four hours out.

locations.blurb: An oasis in a depression 150 metres below sea level — the hottest place in China and one of the lowest points on the planet's land surface. It grows grapes, cools itself with underground irrigation channels, and has two ruined Silk Road cities on its outskirts.
locations.fun_fact: Turpan is watered by karez — hand-dug underground channels that carry snowmelt tens of kilometres from the Tianshan without losing it to evaporation. Some are over a thousand years old.

locations.fun_fact: The Naxi kept Dongba, a pictographic script still in liturgical use — the only living pictographic writing system in the world.

locations.fun_fact: The Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple have stood since the 9th century and survived several earthquakes that flattened everything around them.

locations.blurb: A Tibetan town at 3,200 metres in the far northwest of Yunnan, renamed in 2001 after the valley in a 1933 novel. Cynical branding aside, it is genuinely Tibetan: a working Gelug monastery of six hundred monks, yak pasture and prayer flags at the edge of the plateau.
locations.fun_fact: The town was called Zhongdian until the local government successfully petitioned to rename it Shangri-La, beating several other counties that had applied for the same name.

locations.blurb: The town inside the Li River karst, an hour downstream of Guilin, and the place to actually stay: limestone towers on every side, bamboo rafts on the Yulong River, and enough bolted limestone to have made it the rock-climbing capital of Asia.
locations.fun_fact: The view of the karst on the back of the ¥20 note is at Xingping, a small town about 25 km up the river from Yangshuo.

locations.name: Fenghuang
locations.blurb: A Ming and Qing river town in western Hunan built on stilts over the Tuo River, in Miao and Tujia country. Wooden houses hanging above the water, stepping stones across it, and a covered bridge — one of the prettiest towns in China and, at weekends, one of the busiest.
locations.fun_fact: The writer Shen Congwen, who made this landscape famous in Chinese literature, was born here in 1902 and is buried on the riverbank.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Stay a night. The day-trip buses from Zhangjiajie leave by five, and the town between then and about eight in the morning is worth the detour on its own.

locations.name: Langzhong
locations.blurb: A walled Sichuanese town on a bend of the Jialing River that kept its Tang street grid and about two square kilometres of courtyard houses. It was the provincial capital for seventeen years in the 17th century and has been quietly ignored ever since.
locations.fun_fact: Langzhong is the home of Baoning vinegar, brewed here since the Ming dynasty — the town smells faintly of it, and it goes on everything.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: This is the least-visited of China's four great preserved old towns. Climb Zhangfei Temple's hill for the roofscape and you will very likely be alone up there.

locations.name: Chaozhou
locations.blurb: An eastern Guangdong city with its own language, its own opera, its own tea ritual and one of the great regional cuisines of China. The Guangji Bridge across the Han River is part pontoon and still opens by floating a section of itself aside.
locations.fun_fact: Teochew people emigrated in enormous numbers to Thailand, Singapore and Malaysia, which is why so much Southeast Asian Chinese food is Chaozhou food.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Gongfu tea here is a genuine ritual, not a show — sit down at a streetside table in Paifang Street, accept the tiny cups, and do not hurry.

locations.name: Jingdezhen
locations.blurb: The porcelain capital of the world for a thousand years. Imperial kilns worked here from the Song dynasty onward, the blue-and-white that Europe called 'china' was made here, and the city still runs on clay — with several thousand young potters now working in the old factories.
locations.fun_fact: At its height Jingdezhen was producing porcelain on something close to an industrial scale, with the making of a single piece divided among dozens of specialists.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Saturday and Monday markets at the Sculpture Factory are where young potters sell their own work off trestle tables. It is the best ceramics shopping on earth and it costs nothing to walk through.

locations.name: Qufu
locations.blurb: Confucius was born here around 551 BC and is buried here, and his descendants ran the town for two thousand years. The temple, the mansion and the cemetery form one World Heritage site, and the Kong family tree is among the longest documented lineages in the world.
locations.fun_fact: The Cemetery of Confucius holds the graves of more than a hundred thousand of his descendants across seventy-odd generations.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk the cemetery rather than the temple. It is a huge quiet wood full of stelae, and it makes the scale of the family far clearer than the buildings do.

locations.name: Kaili
locations.blurb: A small prefecture capital in eastern Guizhou that exists, for a traveller, as the door to Miao and Dong country: several hundred villages in the hills around it, each with its own festival calendar, silver work and dialect.
locations.fun_fact: Guizhou's Miao festivals run on the lunar calendar and there are hundreds of them — bullfights, lusheng pipe contests and sisters'-meal gatherings, most of them held for the villages themselves.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Ask at the bus station rather than a travel agency. The rural buses from Kaili go to villages that no tour reaches, and market days rotate through them.

locations.name: Shaoxing
locations.blurb: A canal city south of Hangzhou that produced Wang Xizhi the calligrapher, Lu Xun the novelist and Zhou Enlai's family, and which makes the yellow rice wine that carries its name. Black-awning boats still work the waterways in the old quarter.
locations.fun_fact: Shaoxing wine has been brewed here for well over two thousand years and is the standard cooking wine of eastern Chinese kitchens.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take a wupeng boat through the canals at Bazi Bridge — a stone bridge from 1256 that is still the neighbourhood's crossing — and drink the wine warm, which is how it is meant to be served.

locations.name: Sanya
locations.blurb: The southern tip of Hainan island and China's only tropical resort coast — palms, duty-free malls and high-rise hotels on a run of bays at the same latitude as Hawaii. It is where the whole country goes in February.
locations.fun_fact: Hainan operates the largest duty-free shopping allowance in China, which is a substantial part of why domestic tourists come to Sanya at all.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take the ferry or fast boat over to Wuzhizhou Island early, or drive east to Houhai village where the surfers are — the resort bays are crowded and the coast either side of them is not.

locations.name: Haikou
locations.blurb: Hainan's capital at the north end of the island, and the half of Hainan that is a real city rather than a resort: arcaded colonial shophouse streets, coconut groves, an old-fashioned pace, and the volcanic geopark on its outskirts.
locations.fun_fact: Haikou is built on a volcanic field — the Leiqiong geopark just south of the city has around forty craters, and villages there are built out of black lava rock.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Qilou arcade quarter on Bo'ai Road is unrestored in the best way: families still live above the colonnades, and the coffee shops brew Hainanese coffee thick and sweet.

locations.name: Zhuhai
locations.blurb: The quietest of the original Special Economic Zones — a low-rise garden city of beaches and islands facing Macau across a border you can walk over. Since 2018 the 55-kilometre bridge to Hong Kong lands here.
locations.fun_fact: The Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge is the longest sea crossing in the world, and dives into an undersea tunnel in the middle so ships can still get through.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take the ferry out to Wailingding island for the swimming, or just walk the Lovers' Road promenade at dusk with Macau's towers lit up across the water.

locations.name: Hulunbuir
locations.blurb: The best grassland left in China: a prefecture the size of a country in the far northeast corner of Inner Mongolia, bordering Russia and Mongolia, where the steppe is still grazed rather than fenced. Green from June to August, and forty below in January.
locations.fun_fact: Hulunbuir's grassland is often described as one of the largest and least degraded temperate grasslands anywhere, and it is where Genghis Khan's Mongols came from.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Drive the loop north through Enhe and Shiwei on the Russian border, where Chinese-Russian villages build in log timber and the Argun River is the frontier.

locations.name: Wuzhen
locations.blurb: The most thoroughly restored of the delta water towns, on the Grand Canal between Hangzhou and Suzhou: stone quays, timber houses over the water, indigo cloth drying on frames. It is run as a single ticketed site, which makes it immaculate and slightly unreal.
locations.fun_fact: Wuzhen hosts the annual World Internet Conference, so a 1,300-year-old canal town is also where China's technology policy gets announced.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Buy the ticket for the Xizha section and sleep inside it. The town empties at closing time and the lit canals at eleven at night are what you actually came for.

locations.name: Zhouzhuang
locations.blurb: The oldest tourist water town in China — the one the painter Chen Yifei made famous in the 1980s — an hour from Shanghai, with fourteen stone bridges and a Ming merchant's mansion of a hundred rooms.
locations.fun_fact: The paired Twin Bridges, one arched and one flat, are the image that started the water-town tourism industry after a painting of them was gifted to the United Nations in 1985.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Go on a weekday and go at opening time, before the boats fill. Then walk out to Zhenfeng or the quieter southern lanes where people still wash vegetables off the steps.

locations.name: Xitang
locations.blurb: A delta water town with a particular feature: about a kilometre of covered arcade along the canal, so you can walk the whole waterfront in the rain. Nine rivers meet inside the town and there are more than a hundred lanes, some barely a shoulder wide.
locations.fun_fact: Part of Mission: Impossible III was filmed here, which is why the canal-side arcades occasionally look familiar to people who have never been to China.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Stay overnight — the day ticket crowd is gone by six. Then find Shipi Lane, about a metre wide and a hundred long, and walk it after dark.

locations.name: Tongli
locations.blurb: A water town beside Suzhou, quieter than Zhouzhuang and with the better garden: Tuisi Yuan, the 'Retreat and Reflection Garden', is a World Heritage site in its own right. Fifteen canals, forty-nine bridges, and a working population that still lives there.
locations.fun_fact: Tongli has a museum of Chinese sexual culture in a former girls' school — an unlikely and completely serious institution that was moved here after Shanghai proved awkward about it.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The three linked bridges at the centre — Taiping, Jili and Changqing — are walked in one loop by local couples for luck. Do the loop, then get lost in the eastern lanes.

locations.name: Hongcun
locations.blurb: A Huizhou village at the foot of Huangshan laid out, according to local tradition, in the shape of an ox: a hill for the head, a pond for the belly, and a channel of running water threaded past every door. White walls, black tiles, and art students sketching in every lane.
locations.fun_fact: The fight on the water in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon was filmed at Hongcun's Moon Pond, which is why the village is instantly familiar to people who have never heard its name.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Sleep in the village. The coaches from Huangshan leave in the late afternoon and the reflection in South Lake at first light, with nobody in it, is the whole reason to come.

locations.name: Xidi
locations.blurb: Hongcun's World Heritage twin, ten kilometres away and less painted: a single-street Huizhou village of about 120 surviving Ming and Qing merchant houses, entered through a stone memorial arch from 1578.
locations.fun_fact: Huizhou merchants made their money away from home and sent it back to build these houses — which is why an isolated farming valley contains some of the finest domestic architecture in China.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Go into the houses rather than photographing the outsides. Several are still lived in by descendants who will show you the carved lintels and the light wells the rooms are built around.

locations.name: Wuyuan
locations.blurb: A county rather than a town: dozens of Huizhou villages scattered through terraced hills in northeast Jiangxi, connected by lanes and covered bridges. In late March the whole basin goes yellow with flowering rapeseed and the country's photographers arrive en masse.
locations.fun_fact: Wuyuan is often called the most beautiful countryside in China, and it was administratively part of Huizhou for most of its history, which is why the architecture matches Anhui's rather than Jiangxi's.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Skip the ticketed showpiece villages and stay in Likeng or Qinghua for the covered bridge. Rapeseed peaks in the third week of March; the rest of the year the villages are simply quiet.

locations.name: Zhaoxing
locations.blurb: The largest Dong village in China, in a valley in southeastern Guizhou: about a thousand timber houses on stilts and five drum towers, one for each of the clans that share the site. Rice below, tea on the slopes, and no cars in the lanes.
locations.fun_fact: Dong drum towers and wind-and-rain bridges are built entirely of interlocking timber, with no nails, by carpenters working without written plans.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Stay two nights and walk the terrace path up to Tang'an, the hill village above Zhaoxing. The Dong choral singing you may hear in the evening is a UNESCO-listed tradition, not a performance laid on for visitors.

locations.name: Xijiang Miao Village
locations.blurb: The 'thousand-household Miao village': a whole hillside of dark-timber stilt houses stacked up two slopes above a river in eastern Guizhou, and the largest Miao settlement in the world. It is ticketed and busy by day, and still a working village.
locations.fun_fact: Miao silver work is worn, not displayed — a full festival headdress and collar can weigh several kilograms, and families accumulate it across generations.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk up out of the lower lanes to the viewpoint at dusk when the whole hillside lights up, then eat sour fish soup with a family higher up where the restaurants have no signs.

locations.name: Chengyang
locations.blurb: A cluster of eight Dong villages in northern Guangxi joined by the finest wind-and-rain bridge in China — a covered timber crossing of the Linxi River built in 1912 with five pavilions on it and not a nail in the whole structure.
locations.fun_fact: A wind-and-rain bridge is a roofed social space as much as a crossing: people sit in the pavilions out of the sun, and the bridge is maintained collectively by the villages it links.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Cross the bridge and keep going. The footpaths up through the rice terraces link all eight villages in a morning, and past the first one you will not meet anybody.

locations.name: Cuandixia
locations.blurb: A Ming stone village 90 km west of Tiananmen, built up a mountain amphitheatre in about seventy courtyard houses, most of them from the Ming and Qing. Almost nobody lives there full-time now; the families who stayed run it as guesthouses.
locations.fun_fact: Cuandixia sat on the old caravan road between Beijing and Shanxi, which is why a village of forty households built itself in dressed stone.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Climb the path to the terrace above the village for the plan view — and note the Cultural Revolution slogans still painted on courtyard walls, which nobody has scrubbed off.

locations.name: Shaxi
locations.blurb: A surviving market town on the Tea Horse Road between Dali and Lijiang: a cobbled square with a theatre stage, a Ming temple, an old caravanserai, and a Friday market that draws Bai and Yi farmers down from the valleys.
locations.fun_fact: Sideng Square is the last intact market square left on the Tea Horse Road, the mule-caravan route that carried Yunnan tea to Tibet in exchange for horses.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Come for the Friday morning market. Every other day Shaxi is a quiet village with good bread; on Friday it is the trading town it was built to be.

locations.name: Longji Rice Terraces
locations.blurb: 'Dragon's Backbone': rice terraces stacked from riverbed to ridgeline across a mountainside two hours north of Guilin, worked by Zhuang and Yao families since the Yuan dynasty. Silver water in May, green in July, gold in October, and no machinery at any point.
locations.fun_fact: The Red Yao women of Huangluo village traditionally cut their hair only once in their lives, and some have hair longer than they are tall.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Stay in Tiantouzhai rather than Ping'an — the walk in is longer, the terraces are steeper, and the sunrise viewpoint is above the guesthouses rather than an hour away.

locations.name: Yuanyang Rice Terraces
locations.blurb: Thirteen hundred years of Hani terracing across the Ailao mountains in southern Yunnan — a World Heritage cultural landscape of forest on the ridges, villages below the forest, terraces below the villages, and a water system that has run itself since the Tang dynasty.
locations.fun_fact: The Hani design puts the forest at the top on purpose: it holds the cloud moisture that feeds every terrace beneath it. The whole mountain is one engineered water cycle.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Go between December and March when the terraces are flooded and mirroring the sky. Duoyishu is the sunrise viewpoint; Bada is the one for sunset, and far fewer people bother with it.

locations.name: Hemu Village
locations.blurb: A Tuvan and Kazakh log village in the far north of Xinjiang, in the Altai mountains near the Kazakh, Russian and Mongolian borders — pitched-roof timber houses, hayfields, birch and larch forest, and horses instead of cars for much of the year.
locations.fun_fact: The Tuvans of the Kanas area are one of the smallest recognised communities in China, numbering only around two thousand people across three villages.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Snow closes the road for much of the winter, which is exactly when to come if you can: Hemu under snow, with woodsmoke and horse-drawn sleds, is a different country from the summer version.

locations.name: Jiaju Tibetan Village
locations.blurb: White-and-ochre Tibetan houses scattered up a mountainside above the Dadu River in western Sichuan, in the old kingdom of Gyarong. Each house stands alone in its own barley and walnut plots, so the village is spread across two thousand vertical metres of hillside.
locations.fun_fact: Danba's valleys are also known for their stone watchtowers, some more than a thousand years old and up to fifty metres tall, whose purpose is still argued about.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: In late March and early April the pear and apple blossom comes out across the whole hillside at once. Stay in a family house — most of them take guests, and the top of the village is a serious climb.

locations.name: Yubeng
locations.blurb: A Tibetan village in a hanging valley under the Meili Snow Mountains, reachable only on foot or by horse until recently, at about 3,200 metres. Two clusters of houses, upper and lower, a glacier at the head of the valley and a sacred waterfall above it.
locations.fun_fact: Kawagarbo, the 6,740-metre peak above Yubeng, has never been summited. An attempt in 1991 killed seventeen climbers, and out of respect for local belief climbing it is now banned.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Sacred Waterfall walk is the pilgrims' route — Tibetans circle under the falling water three times. Go slowly; the trailhead is already higher than most people have ever slept.

locations.name: Zhangjiajie
locations.blurb: Three thousand quartz-sandstone pillars standing out of subtropical forest in northwestern Hunan, most of them 200 metres or more straight up. China's first national forest park, part of the Wulingyuan World Heritage area, and the landscape Avatar's floating mountains were drawn from.
locations.fun_fact: The park has a lift bolted to the outside of a cliff — the Bailong elevator climbs 326 metres of rock face in under two minutes and is the tallest outdoor lift in the world.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Everyone rides the elevator and the cable cars. Walk the Golden Whip Stream instead — a flat 7 km path along the canyon floor with the pillars towering over you, and macaques on the railings.

locations.blurb: A Y-shaped valley on the eastern rim of the Tibetan plateau filled with more than a hundred lakes in colours that look retouched — turquoise, cobalt, jade — because the water is saturated with calcium carbonate and full of sunken petrified trees.
locations.fun_fact: Jiuzhaigou means 'nine village valley', after the Tibetan settlements in it. A 2017 earthquake damaged several of the lakes and drained one; the park reopened in stages afterwards.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Go in late October for the larch and maple against the water, and take the shuttle bus to the very top of the valley first, then walk downhill all day.

locations.name: Huangshan
locations.blurb: The Yellow Mountains: granite peaks, twisted pines growing out of bare rock, and a sea of cloud sitting in the valleys below the summits most mornings. This is the mountain Chinese landscape painting is largely about, and it has been climbed by tourists for a thousand years.
locations.fun_fact: Everything on the mountain — food, bedding, building materials — is still carried up on shoulder poles by porters, because the stone stairs are the only way to the summit hotels.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Sleep on the summit. Day-trippers ride the cable car up and down and miss both ends of the day; the cloud sea is a sunrise phenomenon and you have to already be up there.

locations.name: Mount Tai
locations.blurb: The most culturally important of China's Five Great Mountains: emperors came here to make sacrifices to heaven for two thousand years, and 6,660 stone steps climb from the town of Tai'an to the summit temple past inscriptions carved into the rock the whole way up.
locations.fun_fact: Mount Tai carries around 1,800 stone inscriptions, some of them imperial and more than two thousand years old — it is effectively an open-air archive of Chinese calligraphy.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Climb it at night. Chinese pilgrims and students do the stairs in the dark to be at the South Gate to Heaven for sunrise, and the tea houses on the steps stay open for them.

locations.name: Mount Emei
locations.blurb: One of the four sacred mountains of Chinese Buddhism, rising to 3,099 metres out of the Sichuan basin, with monasteries scattered up a two-day walk through cloud forest and a gilded summit statue standing above the cloud line.
locations.fun_fact: The macaques on the pilgrim path are notoriously bold and will go through a bag on the assumption that it contains food. Monks sell bamboo sticks at the bottom for a reason.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk up over two days and stay in a working monastery rather than taking the bus and cable car. Wannian and Qingyin are on the old route and both put up guests.

locations.blurb: One of the deepest river canyons in the world: the Jinsha — the upper Yangtze — squeezed between the Jade Dragon and Haba snow ranges, with nearly 3,900 metres of vertical relief from water to summit. The two-day high trail along its wall is the best trek in China.
locations.fun_fact: The gorge is named for a tiger that supposedly leapt the river at its narrowest point, where the channel closes to about 25 metres.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take the high road, not the new highway on the valley floor. Walk from Qiaotou to Walnut Garden over two days and sleep at Tea Horse or Halfway guesthouse, which has the most famous toilet view in Asia.

locations.name: Li River
locations.blurb: Eighty-three kilometres of river between Guilin and Yangshuo running between limestone towers, water buffalo in the shallows and bamboo on the banks — the single most reproduced landscape in Chinese art, and still a working river with fishermen and ferries on it.
locations.fun_fact: The stretch at Xingping is the view engraved on the back of the ¥20 note, so the most photographed river bend in China is also the one everyone is carrying in their wallet.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The big cruise boats run Guilin to Yangshuo in four hours. A bamboo raft on the shorter Xingping–Yangdi section costs a fraction of that, goes slower, and sits you a hand's width above the water.

locations.name: Kanas Lake
locations.blurb: A long glacial lake in the Altai mountains at the very top of Xinjiang, ringed by Siberian larch and spruce — the only place in China with boreal Siberian forest. The water changes colour through the season with the sediment, and the autumn here is the best in the country.
locations.fun_fact: Kanas is the only place in China where Siberian taiga species occur naturally, and local legend has insisted for generations that something large lives in the lake.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Base yourself in Hemu or Baihaba, the Tuvan and Kazakh log villages rather than the park hotels, and go in the second half of September when the larch turns and before the road closes.

locations.name: Qinghai Lake
locations.blurb: The largest lake in China: 4,300 square kilometres of saline water at 3,200 metres on the northeastern Tibetan plateau, with no outlet to the sea. Tibetan and Mongol herders graze the shore, and in July the rapeseed comes out yellow all the way round it.
locations.fun_fact: Bird Island at the western end is a breeding colony for tens of thousands of migratory birds, including bar-headed geese, which cross the Himalaya at altitudes above 7,000 metres.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Do the loop by bicycle or car over two or three days rather than as a day trip from Xining, and stop at Chaka Salt Lake to the west, where the crust reflects the sky like a mirror.

locations.name: Namtso
locations.blurb: A sacred lake at 4,718 metres, about 110 km north of Lhasa over a 5,190-metre pass — one of the highest large lakes on earth, impossibly blue, with the Nyenchen Tanglha range in snow along its southern shore.
locations.fun_fact: Namtso means 'heavenly lake' in Tibetan. Pilgrims walk the full circuit of the shoreline, which takes about three weeks.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: It is a long day trip from Lhasa and a much better overnight, but sleeping at 4,700 metres is not a small thing — acclimatise in Lhasa for several days first, and expect a rough night.

locations.name: Rongbuk and Everest North Face
locations.blurb: The highest monastery in the world at about 5,000 metres, at the foot of the Rongbuk glacier, looking straight up the north face of Everest. Every British attempt on the mountain in the 1920s and 30s staged through here, Mallory and Irvine included.
locations.fun_fact: The Tibetan name for Everest is Chomolungma. The north-side base camp above the monastery is drivable, which makes this the easiest place on earth to stand at 5,200 metres.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The view is best in the hour after sunrise, before cloud builds on the face. The monastery guesthouse is basic and cold; almost everyone underestimates how cold.

locations.name: Zhangye Danxia
locations.blurb: Striped hills in the Gansu desert: layer on layer of red, ochre, cream and green sandstone tilted on end and eroded into ridges, so the colours run across the landscape in bands. Best in the last hour of light, or just after rain.
locations.fun_fact: The colours are iron and other mineral oxides laid down in a lake basin over roughly 24 million years, then tipped up by the same collision that raised the Himalaya.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The park is walkways and shuttle buses between four viewing platforms. Take the last shuttle of the day to the far platform and wait — the colour arrives in the final twenty minutes and the crowd has gone.

locations.name: Hukou Waterfall
locations.blurb: The Yellow River funnelled from 300 metres wide into a 20-metre stone throat and dropped straight down — the largest waterfall on the river and the second largest in China. It runs thick brown with loess, which is the whole point of it.
locations.fun_fact: 'Hukou' means 'kettle spout'. In spring melt the falls can throw spray high enough to be visible from kilometres away, and the roar is audible before you see the river at all.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Shanxi bank and the Shaanxi bank are separate paid entrances with different views. Flow peaks in the spring thaw and again in the late summer rains; midwinter can be partly frozen.

locations.name: Detian Falls
locations.blurb: The largest waterfall on any land border in Asia, straddling the line between Guangxi and Vietnam — a 200-metre-wide staircase of water in karst country, called Detian on the Chinese side and Ban Gioc on the Vietnamese.
locations.fun_fact: Border marker 53, a French-era stone from the 1890s, sits beside the falls, and there is a small market on the boundary where traders from both countries deal in the open.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take a bamboo raft out to the middle. It goes close enough to the Vietnamese half that you get both countries' cascades in one frame — and the wet season, June to September, is when the falls are full.

locations.name: Fanjingshan
locations.blurb: A 2,570-metre quartzite massif standing alone above the Guizhou hills, with a split rock pinnacle at the top carrying two small temples joined by a footbridge. A World Heritage natural site and the only home of the Guizhou snub-nosed monkey.
locations.fun_fact: Fewer than a thousand Guizhou snub-nosed monkeys exist, and all of them live on this one mountain.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: There are 8,888 steps to the top and a cable car for most of the climb. Go on a weekday — the summit bridge between the two temples takes very few people at once and the queue can be hours.

locations.name: Mogao Caves
locations.blurb: Nearly five hundred decorated cave temples cut into a desert cliff outside Dunhuang between the 4th and 14th centuries — about 45,000 square metres of wall painting and more than two thousand painted sculptures, made by and for people travelling the Silk Road.
locations.fun_fact: The sealed Library Cave gave up around 50,000 documents in 1900, including the Diamond Sutra of AD 868 — the earliest dated printed book in existence, now in the British Library.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Entry is by timed ticket with a guide and a fixed rotation of about eight caves, booked well in advance and capped daily to protect the paintings. Book before you book the flight.

locations.name: Longmen Grottoes
locations.blurb: Two limestone cliffs facing each other across the Yi River south of Luoyang, carved with something over a hundred thousand Buddhist images between the late 5th and 8th centuries — the high point of Tang sculpture, at monumental scale.
locations.fun_fact: The 17-metre Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple was funded partly by Empress Wu Zetian, and the face is traditionally said to be modelled on hers.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Cross the bridge and work back along the east bank in the late afternoon. The big carvings are on the west cliff, so the light comes onto them from across the river as the day ends.

locations.name: Yungang Grottoes
locations.blurb: Fifty-three caves outside Datong holding more than fifty thousand images, carved in the 5th and 6th centuries when the Northern Wei ruled from here. The style is still visibly Indian and Central Asian — this is Buddhist art before it became fully Chinese.
locations.fun_fact: Cave 20's seated Buddha is 14 metres high and open to the weather because the wooden hall in front of it collapsed centuries ago. It has been sitting in the open air ever since.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Combine it with the Hanging Temple and the Yingxian wooden pagoda in one long day out of Datong — a 67-metre timber tower from 1056 with no nails in it, and one of the oldest of its kind anywhere.

locations.name: Leshan Giant Buddha
locations.blurb: A 71-metre seated Buddha carved out of a red sandstone cliff at the confluence of three rivers, begun in AD 713 and finished ninety years later. Its ears are seven metres long, and more than a hundred people could stand on the instep of one foot.
locations.fun_fact: The monk who started it meant the work to calm the river: the rock removed from the cliff was dumped in the water below and did in fact change the currents that were sinking boats.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take the boat rather than the stairs, at least once. The stair queue down the side of the cliff can take hours, and only from the water can you see the whole figure at once.

locations.name: Wudang Mountains
locations.blurb: The home mountain of Taoist internal martial arts, and a range of Ming imperial temple architecture strung along ridges and cliffs — built by an emperor's decree in the early 15th century with over 300,000 workers, and still occupied by Taoist monks.
locations.fun_fact: Wudang is where taijiquan is traditionally said to have originated, and the monasteries still teach it. The Golden Hall on the summit is cast bronze, gilded, and dates from 1416.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Stay on the mountain overnight at Nanyan or the summit, and get up for the monks' morning practice. Day visitors are bussed up and down and never see it.

locations.name: Lhasa
locations.blurb: The Tibetan capital at 3,656 metres, built around the Jokhang temple and under the Potala Palace — a thirteen-storey, thousand-room fortress palace that was the Dalai Lamas' winter seat until 1959. Pilgrims still circle the old city clockwise all day.
locations.fun_fact: The Barkhor is a pilgrimage circuit, not a street: the correct way to walk it is clockwise, and many pilgrims do it in full prostrations, measuring the whole loop with their body length.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Foreign visitors need a Tibet Travel Permit arranged through a tour operator in advance, in addition to a Chinese visa, and it is checked. Give yourself two days doing nothing at all before going any higher.

locations.blurb: Tibet's second city, at 3,840 metres where the Nyang joins the Yarlung Tsangpo, and the seat of the Panchen Lamas. Tashilhunpo monastery above the town still houses hundreds of monks and the tombs of Panchen Lamas going back to the 16th century.
locations.fun_fact: Tashilhunpo holds a 26-metre gilded statue of the Maitreya Buddha, cast in the 1910s and said to have used well over two hundred kilograms of gold.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: This is the staging post for the Everest north side and the Nepal border, and the old town below the monastery — mud-brick lanes, unrestored — is the part travellers skip on the way through.

locations.name: Victoria Peak
locations.blurb: The hill above Central, 552 metres up, with the most photographed skyline view on earth from its northern side: towers, harbour, Kowloon and the New Territories hills stacked behind each other. The funicular tram up has been running since 1888.
locations.fun_fact: Until 1930 the Peak was reserved for European residents by law, and the front seats on the tram were kept for the Governor.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Skip the paid viewing deck at the top of the mall. Walk Lugard Road — a flat, shaded, mostly empty loop around the peak — for the same view through the trees, for nothing.

locations.blurb: The tip of Kowloon: the waterfront promenade that looks back at the Hong Kong Island skyline, the Star Ferry pier, the old clock tower of the Kowloon–Canton railway, and behind it some of the most crowded shopping streets in the world.
locations.fun_fact: The Symphony of Lights, the nightly laser and light show across the harbour, has run since 2004 and involves more than forty buildings on both shores.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk east along the promenade past the Avenue of Stars to the Hung Hom end. Same skyline, no crowd, and the Kowloon Walled City Park is a short taxi from there.

locations.blurb: Among the most densely populated places on the planet: a grid of Kowloon streets each given over to one trade — goldfish on one, birds on another, flowers, sneakers, electronics — with neon overhead and market stalls filling the road after dark.
locations.fun_fact: Mong Kok's population density has been measured at around 130,000 people per square kilometre, which is routinely cited as the highest anywhere in the world.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The specialist streets are the point, and they are best in the early evening: Tung Choi Street for the goldfish, Yuen Po for the birds, and the Temple Street night market a few blocks south.

locations.fun_fact: Apliu Street has been a second-hand and surplus electronics market for decades — the place Hong Kong engineers go for a connector nobody stocks any more.

locations.blurb: Hong Kong's back garden: a fishing town on the east coast with a seafood quay where you buy your dinner out of tanks on the sampans, and behind it a country park of volcanic coastline, hexagonal rock columns and the best beaches in the territory.
locations.fun_fact: The Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark's hexagonal rhyolite columns here are up to 100 metres tall — a volcanic formation on this scale in acidic rock is very unusual.

locations.name: Tai O
locations.blurb: A Tanka fishing village on the west coast of Lantau built on stilts over a tidal creek, with a drawbridge, salted fish drying on racks, and a shrimp-paste works that has been running for over a century. The oldest continuously inhabited settlement in Hong Kong.
locations.fun_fact: Tai O's stilt houses are built over the water on the Tanka pattern, and the village still makes its own shrimp paste — the smell is the first thing you notice getting off the bus.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take the boat out into the channel for the pink dolphins — Chinese white dolphins, genuinely pink, and genuinely endangered by the airport works.

locations.blurb: A dumbbell-shaped island half an hour by ferry from Central with no cars on it at all — bicycles, tiny fire trucks, a fishing harbour full of junks, temples, beaches and a pirate cave. Twenty-odd thousand people live there.
locations.fun_fact: The Cheung Chau Bun Festival ends with competitors racing up a 18-metre tower covered in buns to grab as many as they can; the higher the bun, the more luck it carries.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk the Mini Great Wall path around the southern headland and swim at Tung Wan on the way back. The seafood restaurants along the praya are the reason Hong Kong families come over on Sundays.

locations.blurb: The third-largest island in Hong Kong, also car-free: two villages joined by a footpath over a hill, a power station chimney that ends up in every photograph, seafood restaurants on stilts at Sok Kwu Wan, and beaches most visitors never reach.
locations.fun_fact: Lamma's Sham Wan beach is the last place in Hong Kong where green turtles still come ashore to nest, and it is closed every summer for them.

locations.blurb: Hong Kong's highest point at 957 metres, in the middle of the New Territories — grassland and cloud, and on a clear winter day a view over the whole territory to Shenzhen on one side and the South China Sea on the other.
locations.fun_fact: Hong Kong's coldest recorded temperatures are here, and frost on Tai Mo Shan a few times each winter is enough of an event that people drive up at night to photograph it.

locations.fun_fact: The statue faces north, towards mainland China — unusual, since most Buddha statues face south.

locations.name: Macau
locations.blurb: A Portuguese colony from the 1550s until 1999 and now a Special Administrative Region: baroque church facades and pastel squares in the old centre, the largest gambling economy on earth on the reclaimed land next to it, and Cantonese-Portuguese cooking that exists nowhere else.
locations.fun_fact: Macau's casinos take several times the gaming revenue of Las Vegas, on a territory of about 33 square kilometres.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk the old town on foot, ignore the Cotai resorts for a morning, and eat Macanese rather than Portuguese — African chicken and minchi are the local inventions, not imports.

locations.fun_fact: Taipa and Coloane were separate islands until reclamation joined them in the 1990s. The land the big resorts stand on did not exist thirty-five years ago.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Rua do Cunha is the famous food lane and is packed. Walk two streets over to the Taipa Houses on the waterfront instead, then eat at a Macanese place off the main run.

locations.fun_fact: The original Lord Stow's bakery in Coloane village is where the Portuguese-style egg tart now sold across Asia was adapted, in the 1980s, by an English pharmacist.

locations.name: Bangkok
locations.blurb: Ten million people on a river delta that keeps trying to sink under them, and a city that answers by building upwards and sideways at once: canal houses on stilts, a Skytrain overhead, and a Chinatown that has been trading on the same street since the capital moved here in 1782. The Chao Phraya still does the organising — everything old faces the water, everything new faces the road.
locations.fun_fact: Its ceremonial name is the longest place name in the world: Krungthepmahanakhon Amonrattanakosin Mahintharayutthaya Mahadilokphop Noppharatratchathaniburirom Udomratchaniwetmahasathan Amonphimanawatansathit Sakkathattiyawitsanukamprasit, at 168 letters. Thais use the first word. "Bangkok" is what foreigners kept calling the village that was here first.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Skip the tourist boats. The orange-flag Chao Phraya Express is the commuter service, costs a few baht, and stops at almost every temple you came to see — get on at Sathorn and ride north past Wat Arun with the people going to work.

locations.name: Chiang Mai
locations.blurb: King Mangrai founded it in 1296 as the capital of Lanna, a kingdom that spent most of the next six centuries not being Thailand, and the shape of that decision is still on the map: a square of moat with a gate on each side, about a mile and a half around, with three hundred-odd temples inside and out. The mountains behind it are why the food, the language and the weather are all different from Bangkok's.
locations.fun_fact: Lanna was an independent kingdom, then a Burmese possession for two hundred years, and only became fully part of Siam in 1899. Northerners still speak Kam Mueang, which has its own alphabet, and older temple manuscripts here are written in a script most Thai speakers cannot read.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Wat Umong, in the forest behind the university, is a 14th-century temple built as brick tunnels into a hill — dim, cool, almost empty, and about as far from the moat's tour buses as you can get on a bicycle.

locations.name: Phuket
locations.blurb: Thailand's largest island, joined to the mainland by a bridge, and rich long before anyone came for the beaches — tin was the money here, dredged out of the hills by Chinese labour for a century. The Sino-Portuguese shophouses of the old town were built on it, painted in colours that have nothing to do with the resorts on the far coast.
locations.fun_fact: The island's wealth was tin, not tourism, and the mines only wound down in the 1980s. The Hokkien Chinese families who ran them left the food, the shophouses and the nine-day Vegetarian Festival, which is famous for the entirely non-vegetarian sight of entranced devotees walking through fire.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Thalang Road in the old town, on a weekday morning. Same island, a different century — coffee shops in 100-year-old shophouses, no beach vendors, and the best oyster omelettes on Phuket a few doors down.

locations.name: Ayutthaya
locations.blurb: For four centuries this island between three rivers was the capital of Siam and one of the largest cities on earth — French, Dutch, Portuguese, Persian and Japanese quarters, hundreds of temples, and gilded prangs that visiting Europeans wrote home about in disbelief. A Burmese army burned it in 1767. Nobody rebuilt; the court moved downriver and founded Bangkok, and the brick has been standing in the grass ever since.
locations.fun_fact: At Wat Mahathat a sandstone Buddha head sits at eye level in the roots of a bodhi tree, which grew around it after the sack and lifted it back off the ground. Nobody planted it and nobody moved it there.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Rent a bicycle at the station. The historical park is flat, the ruins are spread over an island you can cross in twenty minutes, and the ones with no coach park — Wat Chaiwatthanaram at the western end, best in the last hour of light — are the ones worth the ride.

locations.name: Railay Beach
locations.blurb: A peninsula on the Andaman coast that is cut off from the mainland by limestone cliffs, so the only way in is by longtail boat — which is why it feels like an island and is not one. Those cliffs are the draw: several hundred bolted sport climbing routes on overhanging pocketed limestone straight above the sand.
locations.fun_fact: At the Phra Nang cave shrine at the southern end, fishermen have long left offerings to a princess spirit believed to control the sea here. The offerings are, and have been for generations, carved wooden phalluses, hundreds of them, stacked up in the mouth of the cave.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk the jungle track between East and West Railay to the hidden lagoon — a rope-assisted scramble up and then down into a tidal pool enclosed by cliff on all sides. It is muddy, it is steeper than it looks, and there is nobody there.

locations.name: Sukhothai
locations.blurb: The first Thai kingdom's capital, from the 13th and 14th centuries, and the source of most of what people mean by classical Thai art — the walking Buddha, the lotus-bud spire, the Thai alphabet itself. It is a park now: ruins in mown grass around lily ponds, laid out inside three rings of earthen wall, and much greener and gentler than Ayutthaya.
locations.fun_fact: A stone inscription attributed to King Ramkhamhaeng, dated 1292, is held to be the oldest example of Thai writing and contains the line that the kingdom had fish in the water and rice in the fields. Scholars have argued about whether it is genuine for over a century; it is on the national curriculum regardless.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Rent a bicycle at the gate — the park is flat, shaded and made for it — and then go 55 kilometres north to Si Satchanalai, the second city of the same kingdom, which is bigger, older-feeling, and where you will meet almost nobody.

locations.name: Pai
locations.blurb: A small Shan town in a valley in the far northwest, three hours from Chiang Mai by a road with 762 curves in it, and a place whose entire reputation rests on being somewhere to do nothing. Hot springs, a canyon, waterfalls, a walking street at night, and mist that sits in the valley until nine in the morning.
locations.fun_fact: The bus company sells anti-nausea pills at the Chiang Mai terminal and T-shirts commemorating the 762 curves at the other end. Both do brisk business.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Rent a scooter and ride out to the Lisu and Lahu villages north of town, or go the other way to the Mae Yen waterfall — a walk that crosses the same stream about twenty times and ends in a pool nobody else has bothered with.
