locations.name: Sumba
locations.blurb: A dry, hilly island south of Flores with almost nothing of the rest of Indonesia about it: villages of high thatched towers built around megalithic stone tombs, an animist religion called Marapu still practised alongside Christianity, and horses everywhere. The south coast has empty beaches with proper surf and almost no one on them.
locations.fun_fact: At the Pasola, held in a few western villages each February or March, two lines of horsemen charge each other and throw blunted wooden spears. Blood spilled on the ground is understood to feed the coming rice harvest, which is the entire point of it.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Sumba's ikat is woven and dyed by hand over months, sometimes years, in natural indigo and morinda root, and the old pieces were grave goods. Buy in the villages around Waingapu rather than in a shop, and expect to be shown the loom.

locations.name: Surabaya
locations.blurb: Indonesia's second city and its biggest port, hot and flat and almost entirely unvisited, which is a fair description of most working cities. It matters here because of what happened in November 1945: an outnumbered, barely armed independence militia fought a British division for three weeks in these streets, lost, and in losing convinced the world the republic was real.
locations.fun_fact: The 10th of November is Indonesia's Heroes Day, and it is Surabaya's. The battle is why the city calls itself Kota Pahlawan, the city of heroes, and why the monument in the middle of it is a 41-metre fluted spike and nothing else.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The House of Sampoerna is a 1913 Dutch building that is still a working clove-cigarette factory, and the free tour lets you watch the hand-rolling floor from a balcony: several hundred women, rolling at a rate that is genuinely hard to follow. Then cross the Suramadu bridge to Madura, which is another world at 5.4 kilometres' distance.

locations.name: Belitung
locations.blurb: A tin island in the Java Sea whose beaches are strewn with granite boulders the size of houses, piled on white sand in clear shallow water — a landscape that exists nowhere else in Indonesia and looks arranged. Inland it is pepper, abandoned tin pits gone turquoise, and coffee shops.
locations.fun_fact: Indonesians know Belitung from Laskar Pelangi — The Rainbow Troops — a 2005 novel about a village school here that became the best-selling Indonesian book ever written and then a film. The island's tourism essentially started the week the film came out.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Manggar on the east coast calls itself the town of a thousand coffee shops and is not exaggerating by much; the local habit is to sit down and be brought coffee without ordering. Then take a boat to Lengkuas island for the 1882 Dutch lighthouse — 18 storeys, and they let you climb it.

locations.name: Bagan
locations.blurb: A plain on a bend of the Irrawaddy holding more than 2,000 surviving Buddhist temples and stupas, built between the 11th and 13th centuries when Bagan was the capital of the first kingdom to unite what is now Myanmar. Over 10,000 were put up in 250 years. Then the Mongols came, the court moved, and the brick was left to the plain.
locations.fun_fact: A 1975 earthquake damaged hundreds of the temples, and the restoration that followed was so free with modern brick and invented spires that UNESCO refused the site for decades. It was finally inscribed in 2019, after a second earthquake in 2016 forced a more careful approach.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Climbing the temples has been banned since 2018 — they are religious buildings and people were falling off them. The purpose-built viewing mounds work, but the better plan is a bicycle and the dirt tracks east of Old Bagan at four in the afternoon, where you will have a 12th-century temple entirely to yourself.

locations.name: Yangon
locations.blurb: Myanmar's largest city and its former capital, laid out by the British on a grid between two rivers and then largely left alone for fifty years — which is why downtown Yangon has the largest surviving collection of colonial-era buildings in Southeast Asia, most of them mouldering, several of them magnificent. Above all of it, on a hill, sits the Shwedagon.
locations.fun_fact: The Shwedagon is plated in real gold — sheets of it, donated by the public and refixed every few years — and the tip of the stupa carries thousands of diamonds and rubies, with a 76-carat diamond at the very top. The tradition holds it is 2,600 years old, which would make it the oldest Buddhist stupa anywhere; archaeologists put the present structure between the 6th and 10th centuries.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Go to the Shwedagon an hour before sunset and stay past dark, when the marble underfoot cools and the families arrive. Find the planetary post for the weekday you were born on — every Burmese Buddhist knows theirs — and pour water over the Buddha there, one cup for each year of your age.

locations.name: Inle Lake
locations.blurb: A shallow lake 880 metres up in the Shan hills, twenty kilometres long, with villages of stilt houses standing in it, monasteries reached only by boat, and floating gardens of tomatoes growing on rafts of matted weed anchored to the bottom with bamboo poles. The Intha who live here have farmed the surface of the water for centuries.
locations.fun_fact: Inle fishermen row standing on one leg with the oar wrapped around the other, which leaves both hands free for the conical net and lets them see over the reeds at the same time. It is done nowhere else, and it is not a show — although a few men at the north end will now pose for one.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take a boat to Indein at the southwestern edge, walk up the covered stairway, and come out among several hundred stupas from the 17th and 18th centuries standing in long grass with trees growing out of them. Hardly anyone on the lake tour goes further than the jetty.

locations.name: Mandalay
locations.blurb: The last royal capital of Burma, founded in 1857 because a prophecy said a great city should be built at the foot of this hill on the 2,400th anniversary of the Buddha, and taken by the British 28 years later. The palace inside its square moat was burned out in 1945 and rebuilt as a replica; the moat and the walls are the real thing, and the hill behind them is still climbed barefoot.
locations.fun_fact: The Kuthodaw Pagoda is often called the world's largest book: 729 marble slabs, each in its own small white stupa, carrying the entire Pali canon of Theravada Buddhism. Reading it at eight hours a day would take you about 450 days.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: U Bein, at Amarapura just south, is a 1.2-kilometre teak footbridge across a shallow lake, built around 1850 from timbers salvaged from the abandoned palace at Ava. Walk it at dawn with the monks rather than at sunset with the boats.

locations.name: Golden Rock
locations.blurb: A granite boulder covered in gold leaf, with a small stupa on top of it, balanced on the very lip of a cliff 1,100 metres up Mount Kyaiktiyo — visibly overhanging, apparently about to go, and not going. It is one of the three great pilgrimage sites of Burmese Buddhism, and pilgrims climb through the night to reach it for dawn.
locations.fun_fact: The rock is said to be held in place by a single hair of the Buddha, enshrined in the stupa above it. Only men are permitted to cross the bridge and touch the rock or apply gold leaf; women make their offerings from the platform.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The open lorries that take pilgrims up from Kinpun are packed to the rails and the road is a series of hairpins — it is half the experience. Stay the night at the top: the crowd thins after dark, the rock is floodlit, and families sleep on mats on the terrace with the lights of the plain below.

locations.name: Hpa-An
locations.blurb: A quiet river town in Kayin State surrounded by limestone karst that comes out of the rice paddy in isolated towers, most of them hollow. The caves inside are full of Buddhas — thousands of small ones set into the walls, some of the reliefs going back to the 7th century — and Mount Zwegabin stands over the whole valley at 722 metres with a monastery on the summit.
locations.fun_fact: At Sadan Cave you walk right through the hill, come out into a hidden lake on the far side, and are rowed back around the outside in a wooden boat. At dusk, at Bat Cave nearby, several million bats pour out of the rock in a continuous ribbon for the best part of an hour.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Climb Zwegabin in the afternoon — about two hours of steps — and sleep at the monastery on top, which asks nothing but expects you to eat what the monks eat. Sunrise over a plain of karst towers standing out of the mist is the reason to be there.

locations.name: Mrauk U
locations.blurb: The capital of the Arakan kingdom from 1430 to 1785, in the hills of western Myanmar, and nothing like Bagan: these temples are squat fortresses of dark stone with slit windows and thick walls, built to be defended as much as prayed in. Villages, rice fields and grazing cattle sit among them, because people never left.
locations.fun_fact: Mrauk U traded with the Portuguese, Dutch and Mughals and was rich enough that a 17th-century Dutch visitor compared it to Amsterdam. The Shite-thaung — the Temple of 80,000 Images — holds a spiral inner corridor lined the whole way with carved figures.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Rakhine State has seen serious conflict and access has been restricted for years at a time; check the current situation carefully before planning anything. When it is open, the way in is the river boat from Sittwe — six or seven hours up the Kaladan, and worth the day on its own.

locations.name: Ngapali
locations.blurb: Seven kilometres of palm-backed white sand on the Bay of Bengal, with fishing villages at both ends and, unusually for a beach with this reputation, almost no development taller than a coconut tree. The catch comes in at dawn and is laid out to dry on the sand a few hundred metres from the hotels.
locations.fun_fact: The name is popularly said to come from a homesick Italian who thought it looked like Naples. There is no evidence for it whatsoever, and everyone repeats it anyway.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Cycle south to Lone Tha village in the late afternoon and watch the boats being pulled up. The seafood shacks on that stretch grill whatever came in an hour earlier, at a fraction of what the hotel will charge for the same fish.

locations.name: Bandar Seri Begawan
locations.blurb: The capital of an oil sultanate on the north coast of Borneo: a small, spotless, alcohol-free city of about 100,000, with two enormous mosques, a museum of coronation regalia, and — out on the river in front of it — a water village of some 13,000 people that has been there for over a thousand years.
locations.fun_fact: Kampong Ayer is the largest water village in the world, a settlement built entirely on stilts and linked by wooden walkways, with its own mosques, schools, clinics and fire station. Antonio Pigafetta, sailing with Magellan, described it in 1521 as a city of 25,000 households built in salt water.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take a water taxi across for a dollar or two — they run constantly, they have no timetable, and you flag one down like a cab. Then ask to be taken out to the Sultan's palace and the proboscis monkeys in the mangroves; the same boatman will usually do it for the price of a coffee.

highlights.name: Sultan Haji Omar Ali Saifuddien Bridge

locations.blurb: Fifty square kilometres of primary rainforest in Brunei's cut-off eastern district, protected as a park and largely closed to everyone but researchers and a controlled trickle of visitors — which is why it is intact. Brunei's oil money meant it never had to log its forests, and around 70 per cent of the country is still under canopy.
locations.fun_fact: The way in was a longboat up the Temburong river until 2020, when the Sultan Haji Omar Ali Saifuddien Bridge opened — 30 kilometres of it, most of it on piles over mangrove and sea, connecting Temburong to the rest of Brunei for the first time by road.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The canopy walkway is an aluminium tower system climbing to about 60 metres, above the tops of most of the trees. Be on it at first light: that is when the gibbons start, and the sound carries for kilometres over unbroken forest.

locations.name: Dili
locations.blurb: The capital of the youngest country in Southeast Asia, on a strip of coast between mountains and the Wetar Strait, with Portuguese churches, Indonesian-era concrete, and a seafront road you can drive the length of in fifteen minutes. Timor-Leste voted for independence in 1999 and became a state in 2002, after 24 years of occupation and four centuries of Portugal before that.
locations.fun_fact: Portuguese and Tetum are the official languages, Indonesian and English are working languages, and there are around fifteen more indigenous languages in a country of 1.4 million people. It is one of only two majority-Catholic countries in Asia.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Climb the 590 steps to the Cristo Rei at the eastern headland early, then walk down the far side to Areia Branca. The Resistance Museum in town is small, hard, and the thing that will actually explain the country to you.

locations.name: Atauro Island
locations.blurb: A steep volcanic island 25 kilometres north of Dili, reached by a ferry that runs a couple of times a week, with about 10,000 people on it living mostly by fishing. The reef starts at the shoreline and drops into water deep enough that whales and dolphins pass through the strait in numbers on their migration.
locations.fun_fact: A Conservation International survey published in 2016 found an average of 253 reef fish species per survey site around Atauro — the highest average ever recorded anywhere in the world.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Stay at one of the community-run eco-lodges on the west coast — Beloi or Vila — where the money goes to the village rather than an operator. Snorkelling straight off the beach is better here than most boat dives elsewhere, and the ferry back on a Sunday is full of people, goats and fish.

locations.name: Mtskheta
locations.blurb: The old capital of the Georgian kingdom, at the meeting of the Aragvi and the Mtkvari 20 km from Tbilisi, and the country's spiritual centre since Georgia adopted Christianity here in the 330s. Kings were crowned and buried in its cathedral for a thousand years.
locations.fun_fact: Svetitskhoveli means 'the life-giving pillar' — the cathedral is said to stand over the robe of Christ, brought back from Jerusalem by a Georgian Jew who was at the crucifixion.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Jvari sits on the bluff above the confluence, and the two rivers meet without mixing — one grey with silt, one clear — for a long way downstream.

locations.name: Svaneti
locations.blurb: A region of high valleys under the main Caucasus ridge, cut off by snow for much of the year and never conquered by anyone — which is why its villages still bristle with defensive stone towers, one per family, built between the ninth and thirteenth centuries.
locations.fun_fact: Ushguli, at 2,100 m, claims to be the highest continuously inhabited settlement in Europe, and its churches held medieval icons and manuscripts that survived because no invading army ever got up here.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Svan language is not Georgian — it split off perhaps four thousand years ago and has no written form.

locations.name: Vardzia
locations.blurb: A cave city dug into a cliff above the Mtkvari in the 1180s under Queen Tamar — thirteen storeys, some six thousand rooms, with chapels, bakeries, wine cellars and a piped spring, all cut into soft volcanic tuff as a refuge from Mongol invasion.
locations.fun_fact: An earthquake in 1283 sheared the outer wall of rock clean off, opening the whole complex to the air like a cut-away drawing — what you see was meant to be hidden inside the cliff.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The main church still has its twelfth-century frescoes, including what may be the only portrait of Tamar painted in her lifetime.

locations.name: Batumi
locations.blurb: Georgia's Black Sea city, subtropical and rainy, where palms and bamboo grow at the foot of the Lesser Caucasus. A belle-époque oil port that has spent the last twenty years growing a skyline of deliberately strange towers along its pebble beach.
locations.fun_fact: The Alphabet Tower is a 130 m double helix with the 33 letters of the Georgian alphabet running up its steel strands — Georgian is written in a script used by no other language.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The botanical garden 9 km north was laid out in 1912 across nine climate zones on a headland; it is the better half of Batumi.

locations.name: Kutaisi
locations.blurb: One of the oldest cities in Europe, capital of the kingdom of Colchis that the Argonauts sailed to for the Golden Fleece, and later of medieval Georgia. Its cathedral crowns the hill above the Rioni and the royal monastery of Gelati is 11 km out of town.
locations.fun_fact: Gelati was founded in 1106 with an academy attached, and its twelfth-century mosaic of the Virgin in the apse is one of the finest pieces of Byzantine-era work outside Constantinople.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The canyons north of town — Okatse and Martvili — are half a day each and far less visited than the monasteries.

locations.name: Geghard
locations.blurb: A monastery in the Azat gorge whose inner churches are not built but carved — hollowed straight out of the cliff, single blocks of living rock with domes cut downward from above, so there is not a seam or a joint anywhere inside them.
locations.fun_fact: Its name means 'spear' — the lance that pierced Christ's side was kept here for five hundred years, and the acoustics of the carved chambers are so exact that a single voice fills them.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Garni, 9 km down the gorge, is a first-century Greco-Roman temple — the only classical colonnade left anywhere in the former Soviet Union.

locations.name: Khor Virap
locations.blurb: A small fortified monastery on a hillock in the flat Ararat plain, a kilometre from the closed Turkish border, and the single most photographed spot in Armenia — because Mount Ararat rises straight behind it, 5,137 m, the national symbol on the far side of a frontier no Armenian can cross.
locations.fun_fact: Gregory the Illuminator was imprisoned in a pit here for thirteen years before converting the king in 301 — which made Armenia the first state anywhere to adopt Christianity.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: You can climb down a ladder into the pit itself. Ararat is usually hazed out by midday, so come at first light.

locations.name: Dilijan
locations.blurb: A forested spa town in the Aghstev valley that Armenians call their Switzerland — deciduous woodland rather than the bare volcanic highland of most of the country, with two thirteenth-century monasteries hidden in the trees above it.
locations.fun_fact: Haghartsin's refectory and churches sit in a clearing so enclosed by beech that you do not see the complex until you are inside it — the site was chosen for exactly that.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Sharambeyan Street in town is a restored block of nineteenth-century wooden balconied houses, with working craft workshops behind them.

locations.name: Gobustan
locations.blurb: A field of tumbled limestone boulders on a semi-desert plateau south of Baku carrying more than six thousand rock carvings — boats, dancers, hunters, aurochs — cut over a span of forty thousand years by people living on what was then a wetter coast.
locations.fun_fact: A Roman inscription here, left by a centurion of the Twelfth Legion in the first century AD, is the easternmost Roman inscription ever found.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Azerbaijan has around half the world's mud volcanoes and a large field of them sits just beyond the reserve — cold grey cones that bubble continuously.

locations.name: Sheki
locations.blurb: A silk town on the southern slope of the Greater Caucasus, terraced up a wooded hillside in red-tiled stone houses, with the summer palace of its eighteenth-century khans at the top of the town inside a walled citadel.
locations.fun_fact: The palace's windows are shebeke — stained glass held in a wooden lattice assembled with no nails and no glue, thousands of pieces per window, still made by a handful of craftsmen in the town.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Sheki halva is a layered pastry of rice-flour threads and nuts, unrelated to the halva sold anywhere else, and is made in the bazaar.

locations.name: Khinalug
locations.blurb: A village at 2,300 m in the high Caucasus, houses stacked so that each roof is the terrace of the one above, reachable until 2006 only on foot or horseback. Its people speak Khinalug, a language related to nothing else and spoken nowhere else.
locations.fun_fact: Around 2,000 people speak Khinalug in total, all of them from this one village — it is among the most isolated languages in the world and has been spoken here for millennia.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The road up from Quba climbs through a gorge and is one of the great mountain drives of the Caucasus; it closes with snow.

locations.name: Almaty
locations.blurb: Kazakhstan's largest city and its former capital, laid out on a grid of tree-lined streets on an alluvial fan with the Trans-Ili Alatau rising 4,000 m directly behind it. Every street running south goes uphill, which is how locals navigate.
locations.fun_fact: Ascension Cathedral, finished in 1907, is one of the tallest wooden buildings in the world at 56 m and came through the 1911 earthquake that flattened the rest of the city.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Medeu, at 1,691 m, is the highest Olympic-size skating rink on Earth and is twenty minutes from downtown by bus.

locations.name: Astana
locations.blurb: A capital built from almost nothing on the open steppe after 1997, when the government moved 1,200 km north from Almaty — a planned city of monuments by Foster, Kurokawa and others, in a place where winter routinely reaches −40 °C.
locations.fun_fact: It is the second-coldest capital city in the world after Ulaanbaatar, and Khan Shatyr is a 150 m transparent tent designed to hold a climate-controlled park inside it through that winter.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The ceremonial axis runs in a dead straight line from Khan Shatyr through Bayterek to the presidential palace — it is meant to be walked, and it takes about an hour.

locations.name: Charyn Canyon
locations.blurb: A 154 km gorge cut 300 m into red sedimentary rock on the edge of the Kazakh steppe — a smaller, older Grand Canyon, its most famous stretch a corridor of eroded pillars that people have called the Valley of Castles for as long as anyone has come here.
locations.fun_fact: A relict grove of Sogdian ash survives on the canyon floor — a tree that has been growing here since before the last ice age and survives almost nowhere else on Earth.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: It is invisible until you are at the rim: the steppe runs flat to the horizon and then simply drops away.

locations.name: Kolsai Lakes
locations.blurb: Three lakes in a staircase up a spruce-forested valley of the northern Tian Shan, at 1,800, 2,250 and 2,700 m, with a pass at the top that drops into Kyrgyzstan. Kazakhs call them the pearls of the Tian Shan.
locations.fun_fact: Nearby Lake Kaindy was created by the 1911 earthquake, which dammed a valley and drowned a spruce forest — the bare trunks still stand upright underwater, preserved by the cold, and break the surface.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Horses are the local transport between the first and second lakes, and are how most of the valley still moves.

locations.name: Turkestan
locations.blurb: The spiritual capital of the Kazakh steppe, built around the tomb of a twelfth-century Sufi poet whose verse carried Islam to the Turkic nomads. Timur ordered the mausoleum in 1389 and it was left unfinished when he died — the scaffolding holes are still open.
locations.fun_fact: Its dome is the largest brick dome in Central Asia, 18 m across, and the building was the trial run for the architecture Timur then built at Samarkand.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Otrar, 60 km away, is the ruined city whose governor murdered Genghis Khan's envoys in 1218 — the act that brought the Mongols west.

locations.name: Baikonur Cosmodrome
locations.blurb: The oldest and largest spaceport on Earth, 6,717 km² of Kazakh semi-desert leased to Russia until 2050. Sputnik went up from here in 1957 and Gagarin in 1961, and for nine years after the Shuttle retired it was the only way any human reached orbit.
locations.fun_fact: It is named after a town 320 km away — a deliberate Cold War misdirection, so that anyone reading a Soviet launch dateline would look in the wrong place.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Gagarin's Start, pad number 1, launched both Sputnik and Gagarin and kept flying crews for sixty-two years before it was finally retired in 2019.

locations.name: Khiva
locations.blurb: The last of the three great Silk Road cities of Uzbekistan and the most complete — an entire walled inner town of mud brick, mosques and madrasas inside 10 m ramparts, preserved whole because the Khiva khanate was the final one to fall, in 1920.
locations.fun_fact: The Kalta Minor was meant to be the tallest minaret in the Islamic world; the khan died in 1855 with it 29 m up, so it stands as a wide turquoise stump — and is the city's emblem.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Juma Mosque has no dome and no courtyard: a flat roof carried on 213 carved wooden columns, some of them a thousand years old, in near-darkness.

locations.name: Tashkent
locations.blurb: Central Asia's largest city, flattened by an earthquake in 1966 and rebuilt by work brigades sent from every Soviet republic — which is why its centre is wide, green, low-rise modernism, with the surviving old town clustered around one enormous domed bazaar.
locations.fun_fact: Its metro, opened in 1977, was built as a nuclear shelter and was a state secret — photography inside was banned until 2018, and every station is decorated to a different theme.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Hazrati Imam library holds the Uthman Quran, a seventh-century manuscript that is among the oldest surviving copies in the world.

locations.name: Shakhrisabz
locations.blurb: Timur's birthplace, over a 1,700 m pass south of Samarkand, where he built a summer palace intended to outdo anything in his capital. Two fragments of its gateway survive, 38 m tall, standing alone in an open square with nothing between them.
locations.fun_fact: The entrance arch of Ak-Saray spanned 22 m — the widest in the Islamic world — and its inscription read 'if you challenge our power, look at our buildings'.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Timur meant to be buried here and had a crypt cut for it; he died in winter with the passes shut and was interred at Samarkand instead. The empty crypt is still open.

locations.name: Moynaq
locations.blurb: A fishing port with no sea. Moynaq was on the Aral shore in the 1960s, canning 25,000 tonnes of fish a year; the water is now 150 km away, and a dozen rusting trawlers sit on the sand where the harbour was.
locations.fun_fact: The Aral was the fourth-largest lake on Earth and lost about 90% of its volume after its two feeder rivers were diverted to irrigate cotton — the seabed left behind is now a named desert, the Aralkum.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The salt and pesticide dust blown off the dry bed reaches the Himalayas; the local rate of respiratory illness is among the highest anywhere.

locations.name: Issyk-Kul
locations.blurb: A lake 182 km long at 1,607 m, ringed by 4,000 m snow peaks and never freezing — the name means 'warm lake', and it is the second-largest alpine lake in the world after Titicaca. It is slightly saline and has no outflow.
locations.fun_fact: A submerged town lies off the northern shore in shallow water — walls, pottery and coins of a Silk Road settlement, possibly the medieval city of Chigu, drowned as the lake level rose.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Cholpon-Ata petroglyph field is a boulder plain of Bronze Age carvings — ibex, snow leopards and hunters — left exactly where they were made.

locations.fun_fact: Its mosque was built in 1907 by Dungans — Chinese Muslims who fled the Qing — as a Chinese temple in wood, assembled without a single nail, and painted in colours that each carry a meaning.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Sunday's animal market starts before dawn on the edge of town and is a working livestock bazaar, not a show — the largest in the country.

locations.name: Song-Köl
locations.blurb: A shallow lake at 3,016 m on a treeless high plateau, reached over passes that are snowed shut for eight months. From June to September herders drive their animals up here and the shore fills with yurts; the rest of the year there is nobody at all.
locations.fun_fact: The summer pasture — jailoo — is the surviving half of Kyrgyz nomadism: the same seasonal migration, the same felt yurts, still done because it is the only way to use this grass.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: There is no electricity and no phone signal on the plateau, and at 3,000 m with no light for a hundred kilometres the night sky is the reason to stay.

locations.name: Osh
locations.blurb: Kyrgyzstan's second city and, at three thousand years, one of the oldest in Central Asia — a Silk Road crossroads at the mouth of the Fergana Valley, built around a five-peaked rock that rises straight out of the middle of it.
locations.fun_fact: Sulaiman-Too has been a place of pilgrimage for a millennium and a half and is Kyrgyzstan's first World Heritage site; Babur, founder of the Mughal empire, built a small mosque on its summit in 1510.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Jayma Bazaar runs for kilometres along the Ak-Buura river and is the largest open-air market in Central Asia.

locations.name: Dushanbe
locations.blurb: A capital that was a village of 3,000 people in 1924 — its name means 'Monday', for the weekly market held there — and was built from scratch as a Soviet city, now a low, hot, tree-shaded grid under the Gissar range.
locations.fun_fact: The national museum holds a 13 m reclining Buddha from the fifth century, found at Ajina-Tepa and the largest in Central Asia — recovered in ninety-two pieces and reassembled over decades.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Hisor Fortress, 30 km west, guarded the road to Samarkand and its gateway and madrasas are the oldest standing buildings near the capital.

locations.name: The Pamirs
locations.blurb: A cold desert of 4,000 m plateaus that Central Asians call the Roof of the World, where the Tian Shan, the Karakoram, the Hindu Kush and the Himalaya all meet. The M41 — the Pamir Highway, second-highest road on Earth — runs 1,200 km across it from Osh to Dushanbe with the Afghan border alongside for hundreds of kilometres.
locations.fun_fact: Its high point, the Ak-Baital pass, is 4,655 m; Lake Karakul below it sits in a 25 km meteorite impact crater and is frozen for more than half the year.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Wakhan branch follows the Panj river with Afghanistan visible across fifty metres of water and the Hindu Kush behind it — villages, fields and people, close enough to wave to.

locations.name: Iskanderkul
locations.blurb: A turquoise glacial lake at 2,195 m in the Fann Mountains, dammed by an ancient landslide, with a 38 m waterfall at its outflow. The name means 'Alexander's lake' — the local story is that his horse drowned in it, and still comes out on moonlit nights.
locations.fun_fact: The Fanns are limestone and shale rather than granite, which is why their lakes run through that range of blues and greens — the colour is suspended rock flour.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The waterfall is a twenty-minute walk downstream from the lake and you reach the top of it before you hear it.

locations.name: Khujand
locations.blurb: Tajikistan's second city, on the Syr Darya at the western gate of the Fergana Valley, and one of the oldest cities in Central Asia — Alexander founded Alexandria Eschate, 'the furthest', on this spot in 329 BC.
locations.fun_fact: Its citadel held out against Genghis Khan in 1220 under Timur Malik, who fought a retreat down the river on rafts; the Mongols levelled the city afterwards.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Panjshanbe — 'Thursday' — is one of the great covered bazaars of Central Asia, a 1950s hall with a painted facade, and it trades every day despite the name.

locations.name: Ashgabat
locations.blurb: A capital rebuilt in white marble between the Karakum desert and the Iranian border — the government has clad hundreds of buildings in Italian marble since the 1990s, on empty ceremonial boulevards, in a place where summer passes 45 °C.
locations.fun_fact: It holds the Guinness record for the highest density of white marble buildings in the world: 543 of them covering over four and a half million square metres.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Old Nisa, 18 km out, is the earth-walled capital of the Parthian empire — the power that fought Rome to a standstill for three centuries.

locations.name: Darvaza Gas Crater
locations.blurb: A 69 m hole in the Karakum desert that has been on fire since at least the 1980s — a collapsed gas field that geologists set alight expecting it to burn out in weeks. Turkmens call it the Gates of Hell and it is the country's best-known sight.
locations.fun_fact: The president ordered it extinguished in 2010 and again in 2022, on environmental and economic grounds; it is still burning, and nobody has worked out how to put it out.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: It is unremarkable by day and extraordinary at night — the standard visit is to camp on the rim, three hours north of Ashgabat on a desert track.

locations.name: Merv
locations.blurb: Five walled cities built beside one another over two thousand years on an oasis in the Karakum — Achaemenid, Seleucid, Sasanian, Seljuk — and by the twelfth century, on some counts, the largest city in the world.
locations.fun_fact: The Mongols destroyed it in 1221 and the chroniclers' casualty figures run into the hundreds of thousands; the site was never fully reoccupied, which is why the plans of all five cities are still legible from the air.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Kyz Kala are corrugated mud-brick fortresses with walls like organ pipes — a Sasanian building type that survives essentially nowhere else.

locations.name: Konye-Urgench
locations.blurb: The capital of Khorezm, sacked by the Mongols in 1221 and again by Timur in 1388, then abandoned when the Amu Darya changed course. What is left stands scattered across open ground: a few mausoleums and the tallest minaret in Central Asia.
locations.fun_fact: The Kutlug Timur minaret is 60 m of fourteenth-century brickwork with no mosque left around it, leaning slightly, standing alone in flat desert.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Turabek Khanym mausoleum's inner dome is a mosaic of 365 segments under a band of 24 arches and 12 windows — a calendar built into a ceiling.

locations.name: Karakorum
locations.blurb: The capital of the Mongol empire for forty years in the thirteenth century, on the Orkhon river in the grassland heart of the country — a city of perhaps ten thousand people administering the largest contiguous land empire in history, then abandoned and quarried away.
locations.fun_fact: William of Rubruck described a silver tree at the khan's palace with four pipes pouring wine, mare's milk, mead and rice beer, worked by a mechanical angel — built by a French goldsmith taken prisoner in Hungary.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Erdene Zuu, built in 1585 from Karakorum's stones, is walled by 108 white stupas; the Orkhon valley around it has been the seat of steppe power since the Turkic khaganates.

locations.name: Lake Khövsgöl
locations.blurb: A lake 136 km long in the northern taiga against the Russian border, holding 70% of Mongolia's fresh water and about 1% of the world's — and connected to Baikal, 200 km away, by its outflow. Mongolians call it the Younger Sister.
locations.fun_fact: It freezes solid enough by February for trucks to drive across it, and the ice can carry two metres of thickness; convoys used the lake as a winter road for decades.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The Dukha, in the mountains west of the lake, are among the last reindeer herders in the world — a few hundred people in perhaps forty households.

locations.name: Gorkhi-Terelj
locations.blurb: An hour and a half from Ulaanbaatar and the easiest place in Mongolia to see the country proper: granite tors standing out of alpine meadow, larch forest, herders' gers, and horses grazing loose all summer.
locations.fun_fact: On the way out stands a 40 m stainless-steel Genghis Khan on horseback, the largest equestrian statue in the world; you take a lift up through the horse and come out on its head.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Many of the gers along the valley are working households that take guests, not resorts — staying in one is the ordinary way to visit.

locations.name: Altai Tavan Bogd
locations.blurb: The five sacred peaks in Mongolia's far west, where the country meets Russia and China at a single point. Khüiten, 4,374 m, is the highest ground in Mongolia, and the Potanin below it is the longest glacier in the country at 14 km.
locations.fun_fact: This is Kazakh Mongolia — the province is mostly Kazakh-speaking, and hunting with golden eagles from horseback is still practised here by a few hundred berkutchi, one of the last places it survives.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The petroglyph complex in the valleys below runs from about 11,000 BC to the Bronze Age — one continuous record of what people here hunted as the climate changed.
